prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B043, Mircea Cărtărescu, as the single credited writer. The reasons are the ones I gave in round 1, tested against the exchange. As publicly described, the Orbitor (Blinding) trilogy and Solenoid have an unmistakable voice. They build recursive, bodily and mnemonic worlds in long, syntactically ambitious prose, with a formal ambition that matches the scale. The project appears to be a single writer's undertaking that runs from the poetry through the large novels. Public accounts suggest the later books extend the earlier ones rather than repeat them. I have not verified that, and I say so below. Compared with the alternatives I weighed, the case for B043 on sustained quality and significance across a body of work is the easier one to argue. Carson's original achievement seems to rest on a few landmark books, and Michon's corpus is deliberately small. I am not counting how many colleagues name B043. All six files give the same literary reasons and the same reservations, so that agreement is no independent check on either. What I change is the citation. The round-1 chair questions and Palm's caution about lineage persuade me to drop the explicit Romanian-poetry lineage and the 'lifetime's work' claim. I cannot show either from the texts, and a citation should not assert more than the evidence supports. The new wording says only that the prose is rooted in poetry, which every file accepts. The poetry becomes the lyric root of the citation, not a co-equal pillar. This matches the thinner translation coverage that Carlberg, Mattson and Sward also record. My own writing about Central European history is context only and not a reason for preferring this writer.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the effect lies in sentence rhythm, syntactic density and digression in Romanian, which I can judge only through translation and critical reports. The long novels may show excess rather than depth, and quality across the whole corpus may be uneven. I could name only Blinding and Solenoid as load-bearing works, and I cannot say which other volumes best show sustained quality. That gap is real and the exchange has not closed it. If readers of the later novels or the poetry said that these repeat or dilute the earlier project, I would lower B043, and I would then compare Carson on original lyric and essay work and Michon on concentration. The inward, maximalist mode may also limit breadth of significance, as Sward argues. I have only partly answered that. Carson remains a serious alternative on formal invention, and Michon on voice. Neither is excluded by hybridity or by a small corpus as such. My reasons for ranking them lower concern the evidence for range and for a whole-oeuvre citation.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu from second to first. He keeps Carson as first alternative, holds that her translations and scholarship are part of one sustained engagement with antiquity and not only a complication, and says the late work of Adonis is less clearly distinguished than the early and middle poetry.
responses.response: Olsson's reading of Carson's translations as feeding her original work is the most persuasive defence of her case in the exchange. I hold it as a real possibility. It does not remove my difficulty. A whole-oeuvre citation has to name an achievement that a reader can locate in the writing, and the connection between translation and original work is the part I cannot confirm from public knowledge. Autobiography of Red and Nox show formal invention. I would be glad to be shown a developing arc in the later books, since that is what would change my ordering. I keep B029 as my first alternative for that reason. On Adonis, I note Olsson's remark about the late work. I cannot test it in Arabic, and I record it as a question for a reader who can.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first but asks whether the inward, maximalist mode limits the breadth of his significance. She ranks Carson last, doubts how hybrid work fits the will's wording on literary work, and wants colleagues who know the later novels to say whether they extend or repeat the project.
responses.response: I take the breadth question as the test most likely to lower B043. The best answer I can give from public knowledge is that the project moves between verse and prose, and between bodily, autobiographical, historical, comic and speculative material. I hold that with caution, since my reading is in translation. That is a claim about range of material, and I do not present it as proof of breadth of significance. I would not use the inwardness as a reason to exclude him, because the interior cosmos is built from the body and from a poetic tradition and is not closed. On Carson I differ from Sward only in degree. Hybrid form does not seem to me to fall outside the will's wording. The open question is how much original work carries the oeuvre. I agree with her that this must be argued from the writing and not from the category.

responses.point: Palm separates sustained ambition from sustained quality. She says the Romanian and European lineage should be argued from the texts and not from reputation, and that the poetry should be treated cautiously in any citation.
responses.response: That distinction is the main reason I changed my wording. In round 1 my citation named Romanian poetry as a source and spoke of a lifetime's work. I cannot support either claim from the texts, and sustained ambition does not establish sustained quality. The revised citation says the prose is rooted in poetry and drops the lineage and the lifetime claim. If the committee wants the lineage in the wording, someone needs to argue it from specific books. I also take her point that the density question separates the two criteria. I cannot settle it from description alone. I record it as the main reservation and not as a settled finding.

responses.point: Carlberg asks whether lower placement of Adonis reflects a judgment about the poetry or the limits of translation. She notes that the same limit applies to Romanian for Cărtărescu and should not be applied selectively.
responses.response: I accept the challenge. I ranked Adonis sixth because I cannot test the language-level claim, not because I judge the poetry weaker. That is a statement about my access and not about the work. The same limit applies to my reading of Cărtărescu in Romanian. I have tried to meet it by keeping the Romanian-language claims out of the citation and by recording the translation dependence as a reservation on both candidates. I cannot treat it as a reason to prefer one over the other. What I can do on B043 is argue from the structures visible in translation: scale, recursion, the link between body and memory. What I cannot do is claim the sentence-level achievement. If original-language readers said that Adonis's formal achievement is stronger than Cărtărescu's, that would be evidence I cannot supply myself, and I would take it seriously.

responses.point: Mattson says a fair assessment must rest on the full oeuvre, including poetry and shorter prose, and would build the citation mainly on the prose. She ranks Michon second and holds that breadth and sustained quality are easier to show for Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I agree with the citation approach, and my revised wording follows it. The prose carries the weight, and poetry appears only as its root. On Michon, I agree that the compression gives a strong claim to a distinctive voice. I ranked him third for that reason and keep him as a second alternative. I come to the same conclusion as Mattson on breadth, though I treat it with caution. A small, concentrated body of work can be a complete achievement. It is harder for a committee to establish, particularly given the translation loss in his syntax and register. I would also like to hear from members who know the later novels about which volumes best show sustained quality, since the exchange has not named any beyond Blinding and Solenoid.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's sentence-level achievement survives translation, and whether the Romanian prose is as sustained as it appears in translated accounts. I have not independently verified any source.
Whether the later long novels extend the earlier project or repeat it. The evidence is public accounts only, and no member has named volumes beyond Blinding and Solenoid.
Whether the poetry and essays, which are thinner in translation, can support a poetry clause in the citation. I have treated poetry as a root and not as a pillar.
Whether the inward, maximalist mode limits breadth of significance. My answer rests on translated material and is held with caution.
How much of Carson's oeuvre is original achievement once translations, adaptations and book-object work are set aside, and whether the later work shows a developing arc.
Whether the late work of Adonis sustains the early and middle poetry, and whether original-language readers could judge it. I cannot judge it myself, and the same limit applies to Romanian.
Michon's small corpus and the translation loss in his syntax limit how confidently his case can be stated.
The 2025 Nobel remarks attributed to me in the profile concern a different laureate. They do not establish my views on any shortlisted writer, and my DN criticism was not surveyed for this stage.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, professional or editorial connection to any shortlisted writer. My work as a critic at Dagens Nyheter and my own historical fiction about Central Europe are context only. They are not evidence of a preference. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated here.
